metadata.title: a-2.2 - Version Control Systems
metadata.description:
Everyone: Make sure you have installed Git (https://git-scm.com/downloads).  
Let's configure your user name and email (they will be recorded in all your commits). Run the following commands on the terminal, adapting the name and email to your own.
git config --global user.name “First Last”
git config --global user.email “myemail@nau.edu”


Everyone: For increased security, GitHub requires using a personal access token instead of your GitHub password to interact via the command line. Follow the steps from the following page to create a personal access token and copy it somewhere (you will need it in the next step). Make sure you give repository permissions to your token. How-to: 
https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/creating-a-personal-access-token 
One group member: Create a new repository on GitHub entitled cs386-a2.2 (only one for the group) and add your teammates as collaborators (you can add them in settings). If a teammate does not have a GitHub account, help them to create one. 
On this repository, create a new file named team.md. Create headings with the names of the teammates in this file (check https://www.markdownguide.org/basic-syntax/ if you don't remember how to format a "heading"). 
Create one issue for each teammate with the title "<name of the teammate> - add personal info to team.md" (including yourself). Assign these issues to the corresponding teammates (you learned how to do this last class). 


Now, let's simulate the workflow you will adopt to develop the team project.

T1.accept: Everyone: Clone the repository into your machine using the git clone command. git clone creates a local copy of a remote repository. The clone includes all the project’s files, history, and branches. Syntax: git clone <https://repository-address>	Remember to use your personal access token instead of your GitHub password. Open the Terminal, go to a folder where you want to clone your repository and clone the repository cs386-a2.2. Write here the command you used:

T2.accept:
Everyone: Let's create a new branch to implement a new feature without messing up with the main trunk. Syntax:
git branch <branch-name> (creates a branch)
git branch -d <branch-name> (deletes a branch)
git branch (lists the branches)
Create a branch with the name "update-teammd-yourname" (obviously replacing yourname with your name). Write here the command you used:

Pro tip: You can checkout and create a branch at the same time with the command: git checkout -b <name-of-your-branch>

T4.title: New Task 4
T4.accept:
Everyone: Use your preferred editor to edit the team.md local file. Add a brief description of yourself under the heading with your name. Be creative :-) 
Now, commit your change, creating a new version of the file in your local repository. We will do this in multiple steps.
git status lists what files were changed.
git add stages a change. Any changes that are staged will become a part of the next commit. 
git commit saves the staged file to the repository, becoming part of the project history. 

Syntax:
git add <file> (stage a file)
git add -A  (stages all files that were changed)
git commit -m "commit message"  (commit the staged files to the active branch)

Run commands to stage the team.md file you've just changed and commit it to the active branch. As the commit message, write "Adding personal info. Fixes #xx", substituting the xx for the issue number assigned to you (see step 3). Adding this instruction will make GitHub close the issue when your change is integrated into the main repository. Besides automating this task, this instruction links the commit and the task description, which is great for keeping a great project history. Write here the commands you used:

git merge <branch-name>  (it will merge branch-name into your active branch)

T8.title: New Task 8
T8.accept:
Everyone: Check on GitHub if your branch is there. Access your branch and create a pull request. A pull request is a request to integrate your change into the repository. 
Add here a screenshot of the pull requests tab showing the pull requests from all teammates.

T9.accept:
Everyone: Assuming you are responsible for peer reviewing in your team, you will review and approve a pull request. Access a pull request from one of your teammates, check the Files Changed tab, and request a change for one of the changed lines (e.g., ask the teammate to change a word). If you are working individually, do it with your own pull request. 
Paste here a screenshot of the comment you are adding to one of the pull requests (one example is enough). When finishing your review, request the change.

T10.title: New Task 10
T10.accept:
Everyone: Check your pull request and see what changes were requested. Implement your change to your local branch and push it again to GitHub. Confirm you implemented the requested changes.
Go through the pull request from the previous item, confirm that your teammate implemented what you requested, and approve the pull request. Once the pull request is approved, the change will be merged into the main branch, and the corresponding issues will be automatically closed (because of the commit message).

T14.title: New Task 14
T14.accept: Repository creator: You want to make sure that no one will change the main branch without the review of at least someone else. Go to the repository settings on GitHub, Branches, Add Rule, and select "Require pull request reviews before merging", "Required approving reviews: 1". This is a common practice in companies to ensure the quality of the code and protect the main branch. Paste here a screenshot of the rule being created.
